opus-5.5.text:
That's actually one of the more interesting things we looked at. Classical LLMs, the autoregressive ones, essentially never tell you a problem is unsolvable. You give them a Blocksworld instance where the goal state can't be reached, and they'll cheerfully hand you a plan anyway, because they're doing approximate retrieval. They're completing the pattern of "here's a problem, here's a plan."

With o1, we saw some improvement. It does sometimes recognize that a problem has no solution, and that's genuinely a step beyond what the earlier models did. But the rate at which it correctly identifies unsolvable instances is still quite low. More worryingly, there's the flip side: it sometimes claims that a perfectly solvable problem is unsolvable. So you can't just take its "this is impossible" at face value either.

And this matters because recognizing unsolvability is, in a sense, the hardest part of planning. To say a plan exists, you just need to exhibit one, and someone can check it. To say no plan exists, you have to have reasoned, implicitly or explicitly, over the whole space of possibilities. A sound planner like Fast Downward can do that and give you a guarantee. o1 gives you no such guarantee.

That's why I keep coming back to the idea of LLM-Modulo frameworks. Whatever o1 is doing internally, it's still not something you can trust on its own for these questions. It's better to pair it with external verifiers that can actually certify correctness. The improvement is real and worth acknowledging, but it's not the same thing as having a reasoner you can rely on. And of course, the cost of all those reasoning tokens is another dimension people tend to forget when they compare it against classical planners that solve these problems essentially for free.

fable-5.1.text:
So this is actually one of the more revealing experiments we did. When we looked at o1 on planning problems, the headline was that it did much better than the plain LLMs on things like Blocksworld, and people got very excited about that. But then we asked a simple question: what happens when the problem has no solution at all?

And this is important, because a real planner, a classical planner, will tell you "this goal is unreachable." That's part of what it means to actually reason about the problem. You explore the space, you exhaust it, and you say no plan exists. So we constructed Blocksworld instances where the goal was unsatisfiable, sometimes in fairly obvious ways, like asking for block A on B and B on A at the same time.

What o1 did, most of the time, was just confidently hand you a plan. It would produce a sequence of actions, very fluently, that of course doesn't achieve anything, because nothing can. And in the small number of cases where it did say the problem was unsolvable, when we checked those claims, a good fraction of them were wrong in the other direction, it was calling solvable problems unsolvable. So it wasn't that it had learned to detect infeasibility. It was more like it had learned that "this is unsolvable" is sometimes an acceptable thing to say.

To me that's the key thing about these so-called reasoning models. They are approximate retrievers that have been given some kind of reinforcement learning over chains of thought, and that improves the hit rate on problems that look like the training distribution. But improved hit rate is not the same as a guarantee, and unsolvable problems are exactly where the difference shows up. Verification is where you need soundness, and o1 doesn't give you that. If you want that property, you still need an external verifier, which is why I keep arguing for these LLM-Modulo type architectures, where the model generates and something with actual semantics checks.

And the other thing I'd point out, which people underestimate, is that you can't see what o1 is doing. OpenAI hides the reasoning tokens. So when it fails on an unsolvable problem, you have no diagnostic trace, you just have a wrong answer and a bill for however many thousand tokens it burned before giving it to you. That's not a great trade when a classical planner would have told you "no solution" in milliseconds.

astra-6.text:
The important distinction is between finding a plan and recognizing that no plan exists. If a system fails to find a solution, that doesn’t establish that the problem is unsolvable. It may simply have searched badly or run out of resources.

So I would assess O1 by asking what supports its conclusion. If it produces a plan, we can check whether the actions are legal and whether they reach the goal. If it says there is no solution, we need a different kind of justification—perhaps an invariant showing that the goal cannot be reached, or a complete search that exhausts the possibilities. A long explanation is not, by itself, such a justification.

That’s why unsolvable instances are an important test. Does the model recognize a contradiction, keep trying indefinitely, or quietly relax a constraint and give you an answer to a different problem? I wouldn’t infer reliable handling of unsolvability from better performance on solvable problems. The useful arrangement is to let the model propose ideas and have a sound reasoning procedure establish whether those ideas actually settle the question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think unsolvable problems are a very important test, because there’s a distinction between finding a plan and establishing that no plan exists. If a system fails to find a plan, that doesn’t mean the problem is unsolvable. It may simply have failed to find one.

So with O1, I would ask: does it correctly recognize that the goal cannot be reached, and can it justify that conclusion? Or does it keep trying and eventually produce something that looks like a plan but violates the constraints? More time spent reasoning doesn’t, by itself, give you a guarantee of correctness.

This is where a sound external verifier or planner becomes valuable. The language model can propose ideas, but we need a principled way to check the plans—and a stronger basis for declaring that no plan exists.
